newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai C/A gap to limit investment - minister.
newsitem.headline: Thai C/A gap to limit investment - minister.

text.p: Thailand's wide current account deficit will limit its investment in capital-intensive, basic industries such as steel and petrochemicals in the next five years, caretaker Industry Minister Kosit Panpiemrat said on Wednesday.

A more liberalised global and regional trade policy which will eventually reduce government protection on various industries as well as oversupply of such products will also exacerbate the problem facing these sectors in the future, Kosit told a seminar on Thailand's first industry masterplan.

Under the plan which covers 1997-2001, the Thai government will instead back the expansion of small and medium-sized businesses as well as supporting industry such as parts and components, Kosit told industry officials.
"The wide current account gap will force us to be more selective in borrowing money for investment. We will continue to support big projects which are funded by Foreign Direct Investment," he said.
"Our industry is facing structural problem and we need the masterplan to deal with it," he said.
Thai industrial goods exports during the first half of 1996 grew only five percent year-on-year compared with 25 percent during January-June 1995.

The masterplan calls for prioritising of investment, increasing quality and efficiency of Thai industry, boosting supporting industry as well as small- and medium-sized industry, and issuing anti-dumping law to protect local industry.

Thailand's current account deficit, or a gap between saving and investment, stood at 8.1 percent of gross domestic product in 1995. Some economists forecast that it will be higher this year even though the Bank of Thailand's forecast put it at 7.8 percent of GDP.
"We will have to save more in order to be able to rely more in our own saving for investment," he said.
Prime Minister-designate Chavalit Yongchaiyudh said in his new government Thailand will be more careful in spending on mega-projects.

"The most important thing is to have deciplined fiscal policy...We will review mega-projects and will see if they have good economic return. We are not going to spend for nothing,' he told foreign reporters on Tuesday.
